site.name: atlas-tutor
site.summary: atlas-tutor Fictional AI math & CS tutor "Atlas Tutor" chat fixture. UXBench fixture in the Chatbot / Agent Interface category. Layout **Three-column desktop:** - **Left rail (260 px)** — branded sidebar with New-chat button, search, Subjects nav (Mathematics / Programming / Physics / Statistics / Linear algebra with counts), and threaded history grouped by recency (Today / Last 7 days / Earlier — 11 threads total). Sticky profile-mini footer with streak badge. - **Center (flex)** — conversation viewport with sticky head ("Chain rule — when both functions move" · model · last reply · 3 head-tools); messages area centered to 820 px; sticky composer at the bottom with attach / textarea (Cmd+Enter to send) / mic / send-button row plus suggestion chips and a model selector. - **Right rail (320 px)** — practice problems panel (6 chain-rule problems with difficulty pills / hint button / 3-state Solve→Submit→Correct toggle), Concepts card (4 internal links), Your progress card with progress bar updated as practice is completed. Conversation pre-fill

run_plan.goal: Exhaustively explore the single-page Atlas Tutor chat experience, with emphasis on the primary settings/privacy entry point and adjacent conversation, practice, navigation, and responsive states visible in the prescan.
run_plan.summary: The run should treat index.html as a dense app-like surface rather than a multi-page site, starting with baseline verification of the three-column desktop layout and then exercising the core learning flow: history/navigation, active conversation tools, composer/suggestions, and the right-rail practice workflow. Because only one HTML page is known, coverage should focus on state changes and overlays that may be triggered in-page, especially the settings gear, practice controls, concept links, and message actions. Repeat the most important interaction paths on mobile, where the prescan already shows many undersized tap targets.
assumptions: Only index.html is known from the prescan, so any settings/privacy experience is likely exposed as an in-page panel, modal, drawer, or anchored section rather than a separate HTML page.
Many visible controls use href '#' or button elements, so significant behavior may happen client-side without navigation.
The primary product flow is tutoring around an existing conversation, with adjacent flows for new chat, search/history recall, practice problems, and profile/settings access.
Mobile risk is high because multiple controls in the header, message actions, and sidebar/footer are already flagged as small tap targets.
risk_hotspots: Settings gear (⚙) in the left footer/profile area: likely entry to the requested settings/privacy flow and may open a hidden modal/drawer
Header tools (⌥ Steps, ▶ Practice, ⋯): compact controls that may reveal important state changes or menus
Practice problem cards in the right rail, especially the Solve → Submit → Correct multi-state interaction and progress updates
Composer row: attachment, textarea, mic, send button, model selector, and Cmd+Enter hint/state
Search chats input with threaded history groups: filtering, result clarity, and recovery back to full history
Message action row (👍, 👎, Share, Copy, Try again): feedback/state persistence and crowded mobile usability
Concept links card on the right rail: internal anchors or in-page context changes that may alter the current lesson
Suggestion chips below the composer: quick prompt insertion/send behavior and topic switching
New chat button and threaded history items: context switching, selected-state accuracy, and unsaved draft handling if present
Mobile versions of small controls: ⚙, ⋯, reaction buttons, share/copy/retry, and top action buttons

phases.title: Desktop baseline and app structure
phases.objective: Confirm the initial desktop information architecture, sticky regions, and visible affordances before changing state.
key_checks: Verify the three-column layout is present: left rail, central conversation, right practice rail
Inspect sticky behavior of the conversation header and bottom composer during scroll
Record the default selected thread, selected subject, and visible right-rail lesson alignment with the active conversation
Check whether the left footer profile mini and settings gear remain accessible while scrolling
Note any initially hidden content below the fold, including full practice panel and concepts/progress cards
exit_criteria: Initial desktop structure and major regions have been visually confirmed
At least one full-page scroll validates sticky header/composer behavior and reveals lower right-rail content

phases.title: Settings/privacy and top-level controls
phases.objective: Prioritize discovery of the settings/privacy flow and validate related global controls exposed from the shell.
key_checks: Activate the ⚙ settings control and inspect whether it opens a settings/privacy panel, modal, menu, or navigates within the page
If settings opens, explore privacy-relevant sections, toggles, close behavior, focus handling, and return path to the conversation
Open the ⋯ overflow control to discover hidden global actions if present
Toggle or open ⌥ Steps and ▶ Practice from the header to understand whether they switch modes, scroll the page, or reveal supplemental UI
Validate keyboard or pointer dismissal paths for any overlay, drawer, or modal opened from these controls
exit_criteria: The settings/privacy entry path has been either exercised or conclusively determined absent/inert
All visible top header/global controls have been clicked once and their outcomes documented

phases.title: Conversation and composer workflow
phases.objective: Test the core tutoring interaction flow around existing messages, quick prompts, and reply actions.
key_checks: Use one or more suggestion chips to confirm whether they populate the composer, send immediately, or alter topic context
Type into the main textarea and use the send button to test message submission and any loading/reply state that appears
Try the attachment and mic controls to determine whether they open menus, show permissions messaging, or remain inert
Inspect the model selector near the composer if interactive and verify whether model choice changes visible state
Exercise message actions on the assistant response: thumbs up, thumbs down, Share, Copy, and Try again
Check whether Copy provides feedback, Share opens a native/custom share flow, and Try again duplicates/regenerates content without breaking scroll position
exit_criteria: At least one composer-originated interaction and at least three message-level actions have been exercised
Observed outcomes for chips, send flow, and auxiliary composer controls are captured

phases.title: Navigation, history, and lesson context switching
phases.objective: Validate how users move across subjects, prior threads, search results, and concept links without losing orientation.
key_checks: Use the Search chats input to filter history and then clear/recover the full list
Open several history threads across Today, Last 7 days, and Earlier to verify selected-state updates and conversation/context changes
Switch among subject categories such as Mathematics, Programming, Physics, Statistics, and Linear algebra to see whether they filter or navigate
Click the Atlas Tutor brand/home affordance to see whether it resets the current state
Open the concept links card items (Chain rule, Derivatives of trig functions, Composing functions, Notation: f', dy/dx, ḟ) and observe whether they scroll, replace context, or open subviews
Use + New chat and assess whether it clears the conversation, creates a draft state, or changes the right rail
exit_criteria: Search, history switching, subject switching, and concept-link behavior have each been tested at least once
A recovery path back to the original or a stable conversation state has been verified

phases.title: Practice workflow and progress tracking
phases.objective: Deeply validate the right-rail problem-solving experience and its integration with progress/state.
key_checks: Inspect all visible practice cards, including difficulty pills and problem numbering, for consistency and readability
Use Hint on at least one easy and one harder problem to verify hint reveal behavior and repeatability
Exercise the Solve control on multiple problems and confirm the documented 3-state Solve → Submit → Correct sequence if implemented
Check whether solved/submitted states update the Your progress card and progress bar
Confirm that practice interactions do not unexpectedly reset the main conversation or cause layout jumps
Test whether the header ▶ Practice button synchronizes with the right-rail panel or moves focus to it
exit_criteria: At least two practice problems have been interacted with through meaningful state changes
Progress behavior and any coupling between practice and conversation have been observed

phases.title: Mobile responsive validation
phases.objective: Repeat critical flows on mobile to assess navigation, density, discoverability, and tap-target risks already indicated by the prescan.
key_checks: Verify how the three-column desktop layout collapses on mobile and whether left/right rail content remains discoverable
Repeat access to settings/privacy from the ⚙ control on mobile
Repeat one conversation action path: open a thread, type or use a suggestion chip, and send or attempt send
Repeat one practice interaction and confirm whether hints/solve states are usable in the mobile layout
Inspect tap usability of small controls including header buttons, overflow, reactions, Share, Copy, Try again, and settings
Check for clipped text, overlap, off-screen drawers, hidden sticky composer issues, and horizontal scrolling
exit_criteria: Critical settings/chat/practice flows have each been attempted once on mobile
Responsive issues and mobile-specific blockers have been identified for the highest-risk controls

coverage_targets.pages: Visit the only known HTML page (index.html) and explore all major in-page states, panels, and overlays it exposes.
coverage_targets.features: Exercise most visible controls on the shell, conversation, composer, navigation/history, and practice rail; prioritize settings/privacy, top tools, search, new chat, concept links, and multi-state practice interactions.
coverage_targets.mobile: Repeat the highest-value checks on a mobile viewport, especially settings access, a basic chat interaction, history/navigation access, and at least one practice interaction, with special attention to the prescan's small tap targets.

notes: Do not assume external pages or account/auth flows exist; stay grounded in in-page interactions unless a control explicitly navigates.

Because the explored goal mentions settings/privacy but the prescan only shows a gear icon, the run should spend early steps discovering whether privacy controls are actually implemented behind that entry point.
If controls are inert, document that clearly rather than forcing speculative flows.

observation.title: Atlas Tutor — math & CS tutor
observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Explain Markov chains ⌘↵ to send · model · Atlas-3 ↓ PRACTICE PROBLEMS Chain rule Difficulty · level 2 1 EASY d/dx sin(3x + 2) Solve 💡 Hint 2 EASY d/dx (x² + 1)5 Solve 💡 Hint 3 MEDIUM d/dx e^(cos(x)) Solve 💡 Hint 4 MEDIUM d/dx tan(√x) Solve 💡 Hint 5 HARD d/dx ln(sin(x³)) Solve 💡 Hint 6 HARD d/dx (sec(2x))3 Solve 💡 Hint Concepts in this thread Chain rule Calculus · 5 min Derivatives of trig functions Calculus · 3 min Composing functions Pre-calc · 4 min Notation: f', dy/dx, ḟ Calculus · 2 min Your progress Today 4 / 10 problems Streak 14 days · 🔥 Topic mastery Chain rule · 72%

Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA tan(√x) — derive it A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like tan(√x) — derive it, write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. Open practice problem #3 on the right and try this same recipe. 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Explain Markov chains ⌘↵ to send · model · Atlas-3 ↓ PRACTICE PROBLEMS Chain rule Difficulty · level 2 1 EASY d/dx sin(3x + 2) Correct 💡 Hint Hint · identify the outer and inner functions in sin(3x + 2). Differentiate each separately, then multiply. 2 EASY d/dx (x² + 1)5 Solve 💡 Hint 3 MEDIUM d/dx e^(cos(x)) Solve 💡 Hint 4 MEDIUM d/dx tan(√x) Solve 💡 Hint 5 HARD d/dx ln(sin(x³)) Solve 💡 Hint 6 HARD d/dx (sec(2x))3 Solve 💡 Hint Co

Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA tan(√x) — derive it A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like tan(√x) — derive it, write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean!
